title: Keep my Sikhs
hookLine: sevak sikh hamaare taareeh: carry my servants and Sikhs across (Chaupai)
tomorrow: The one who spreads and gathers

lines: ONE BOAT, ONE PERSON TO STEER.
cards: A wide river in flood, the kind people in Punjab knew well, brown and fast and far too deep to wade. On this bank, everyone you love. On the far bank, safety.
There's one boat, and one person who knows how to steer it. You don't ask for yourself first. You ask for them: take my mother, take my friend, take the kids.
Get them across. That picture of a river and a crossing runs all through Sikh scripture, and in Chaupai the Guru uses it to pray for his people.

teach.b: The line is sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi. Sevak: servants, those who serve. Sikh: learners, disciples.
Hamaare: mine. Taareeahi: carry them across.
The verb is from taarna, to ferry over, to bring someone safely to the other shore.
In the Guru Granth Sahib, the world is often pictured as a vast, terrifying ocean, and the Guru, or the Name, as the boat that carries people over it.
So the Tenth Guru is doing something tender here: a Guru praying for his disciples, asking God to carry them across.

teach.h: THE CIRCLE WIDENS: ME, FAMILY, SIKHS.
teach.b: Look how the prayer's circle has widened. First, protect me. Then, may my family live in peace.
Then, all my servants and Sikhs. Sikh prayer often widens like that.

The Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, names the Gurus, the martyrs, the community, and ends by asking for the good of all, everyone, without exception. You met that on day three hundred thirty.
One more thing. This prayer is said by the community itself, every morning and evening.

teach.h: A PRAYER THE GURU PRAYED FOR THEM.
teach.b: So a Sikh reciting it is saying a prayer the Guru prayed for them.
Carry them across lands differently when you know you're one of the them.

how: Many Sikhs recite this line within Chaupai Sahib daily; Sikh prayer, especially the Ardas, typically widens from oneself to family, community and finally the good of all.

o: the Gurus who came before the Tenth
servants and disciples, the Guru's people
soldiers who guarded the Guru's town

games.q: keep my Sikhs — tap the pairs.
p: the river the Name carries people over
the good of all, at the Ardas's end

s: in this line the Guru prays for his disciples
carry my servants and Sikhs across: a Guru asking God to carry his own people across.
Chaupai's circle of prayer stays on the one praying
it widens: me, my family, my servants and Sikhs.
the river crossing image is found only in Chaupai
the Guru Granth Sahib often pictures the world as an ocean and the Name as the boat across it.

games.q: you're the Guru. you've asked for your own protection and your family's peace. who does the prayer turn to next?
o: only the rulers of the land.
my servants and Sikhs: carry them across.
no one else: the prayer is finished.
games.why: sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi: carry my servants and Sikhs across. the circle keeps widening, the way Sikh prayer does.

practice: Bring to mind one friend in a hard river right now, illness, grief, a bad job, a lonely stretch; see their face and say their name quietly.
If you pray, hold that name in Waheguru or say the line, carry them across; if not, hold them in your attention and wish them safely to the other bank.
Then, if it feels right, let the circle widen: one more name, then everyone in a river like theirs.

wordCard.voice: Sevak sikh, servants and disciples. Hamaare taareeahi: carry them across, the Guru praying for his people over the river.
